title: Arrive Composed: What to Expect from a Chauffeur-Driven Airport Transfer
excerpt: A long flight ends more gently when the next step is already arranged. Here is how a chauffeur-driven transfer works, and what to have ready.
content:
A flight is rarely the tiring part of a journey. The tiring part tends to come afterwards: the queue, the search for a ride, the negotiation over the route, the uncertainty about whether you will reach your first appointment looking like someone who has slept. A chauffeur-driven airport transfer removes most of that. It replaces a series of small decisions with one arrangement made in advance.

If you have never booked one, or you are arranging one for a guest, this guide walks through what is useful to know before you land.

Start with the details that matter

A good transfer begins with clear information. The more complete your request, the fewer messages you will need to exchange later. Have these ready when you get in touch:

  • Your airport. In Nairobi, that usually means Jomo Kenyatta International (JKIA) or Wilson Airport.
  • The direction of travel. Are you being collected from the airport, or taken to it?
  • Your flight number and time. A flight number is especially helpful for arrivals, because it identifies exactly which flight to follow.
  • Passengers and bags. Four people with suitcases need a different car from one person with a laptop bag.
  • Where you are going. The area or address at the other end of the trip.

If you are booking for someone else, include their name and tell the transfer company how you would like them to be contacted. It is a small courtesy that prevents confusion at a busy terminal.

Choosing the right car

The right car depends on who is travelling and what happens next. An executive sedan suits a business traveller heading straight to a meeting. A larger SUV makes sense for a family, for several suitcases or for a group who would rather stay together. If you are welcoming an important guest, the car is part of the welcome, and it is worth choosing with that in mind.

Think about the end of the journey as well as the start. A long drive out of the city, a hotel with a formal entrance and a narrow residential street all favour slightly different vehicles. Mention your destination and ask for a suggestion if you are unsure.

What happens when flights change

Flights run late, and sometimes they run early. The most useful thing you can do is keep the people arranging your transfer informed. Send a message as soon as you know about a change, and give them the new time if you have it.

It is sensible to ask, when you book, how changes and delays are handled, so that you know what to expect. Do not assume every provider treats them the same way. Your quote and booking confirmation are the place to settle those details.

Using the time well

One of the quiet advantages of being driven is that the journey becomes usable. Some travellers reply to the messages that arrived during the flight. Others go over the notes for a meeting. Plenty of people simply look out of the window, which is a perfectly good use of a first hour in a city.

If you need a quiet ride, say so. If you would like a stop on the way, mention it when you book, so that it can be planned for and included in your quote.

Heading to the airport

Departures deserve the same care as arrivals, perhaps more, because the cost of running late is higher. When you arrange a drop-off, share your flight time and let the provider advise on a sensible pick-up time. Nairobi traffic is difficult to predict, so it is wise to leave generous room.

Before you step out of the car, do a quick check of the seat pockets and door bins. Phones, passports and chargers have a way of hiding there.

A short checklist

  1. Confirm your flight details, and double-check the date if you land just after midnight.
  2. Send your request with passenger and luggage numbers.
  3. Read your confirmation and quote, and ask about anything that is not clear.
  4. Save the contact number somewhere you can reach it without Wi-Fi.
  5. Tell your provider if anything changes.

None of this is complicated, which is rather the point. A well-arranged transfer should feel like very little at all. You walk out, you are looked after, and you arrive composed.

title: Planning Your Wedding Cars: A Simple Timeline and Checklist
excerpt: Wedding transport is easy to leave until late and hard to fix at the last moment. A calm order of work, from first idea to the big day.
content:
Wedding cars tend to arrive on the to-do list somewhere between the flowers and the seating plan, and they are often treated as a detail. Yet the car is in the photographs, it carries the people who matter most, and it decides whether the day begins calmly. A little planning goes a long way.

This is a simple order of work. Adapt it to the size of your celebration and how far ahead you are planning.

As soon as your date and venues are set

Popular dates fill quickly, so the first step is simply to ask. You do not need every detail to begin a conversation. You need your date, a rough idea of your venues and an estimate of how many cars you have in mind.

Think about who actually needs transport. The usual list includes the bride, the groom, the bridal party, parents and any elderly relatives. Some couples add a car for guests of honour or a convoy for the photographs. Writing the names down will quickly tell you how many vehicles you need.

Choosing the look

A matching convoy makes a strong impression, particularly in photographs and on the road between venues. A single standout car can be just as memorable if your celebration is more intimate. Consider your venues, too. A long gravel drive, a garden on a hillside or a narrow city entrance may each favour a different kind of vehicle.

If you would like the cars dressed for the day, say so early. Ribbons and flowers need to suit your colours, and it helps to share a photograph of your theme or bouquet. Ask what is possible, and agree the details and the cost before you confirm.

Once your programme takes shape

When your ceremony time is settled, map out the movement of the day. A simple table works well, with four columns: who, from where, to where, and by when. Add every leg, including those that are easy to forget:

  • The trip from the home or hotel to the ceremony
  • The move from the ceremony to the photo location
  • The arrival at the reception
  • The couple's departure at the end of the night

Be realistic about the time between stops. Weddings run on their own clock, and receiving lines, family photographs and long hugs all take longer than expected. Leave room for the day to breathe.

Closer to the day

Share your final programme with your car provider, along with exact addresses or map pins for each stop. Include the name and number of one person who can make decisions on the day. This should not be the bride, the groom or either of their mothers. A trusted friend or your planner is a far better choice.

Check the arrangements with your venues, too. Ask where the cars can wait, where they can turn, and whether anyone needs to be told they are coming.

The day before

A short message to confirm the plan is all you need. Check the pick-up time for the first car, and make sure your coordinator has the numbers saved. Then put your phone down. The transport has been handled.

On the day

Allow more time than you think for getting dressed, because that is where most weddings begin to run late. Let your coordinator deal with the cars, so that any small change stays away from you. When the door opens and the convoy is waiting, take a moment. It is one of the pictures you will keep.

Your wedding car checklist

  1. Note your date, venues and a list of who needs transport.
  2. Request availability and choose your cars.
  3. Agree on any decoration, and share your colours.
  4. Build a simple movement plan for the day.
  5. Confirm your quote and exactly what it covers.
  6. Send final timings, addresses and a coordinator's number.
  7. Check the access and waiting areas at each venue.
  8. Reconfirm the day before.

Small touches that people remember

Consider a bottle of water and a few tissues in the car for the couple, a playlist for the short ride between venues, and a moment for the two of you alone before stepping out to greet everyone. These cost almost nothing, and they are often what people recall first when they look back on the day.

title: Executive Sedan or Luxury SUV? Matching the Car to the Occasion
excerpt: Sedans and SUVs send different signals and solve different problems. A plain guide to which suits which moment.
content:
A car says something before you do. It sets a tone at the kerb, shapes how you feel when you step out and decides how comfortable the journey will be. When people choose a rental for an important occasion, the decision often comes down to a familiar pair: the executive sedan or the luxury SUV.

Both can be excellent choices. They simply do different jobs, and the most useful question is rarely which car is more impressive. It is which car suits the people inside it, the road ahead and the moment when the door opens.

The case for the executive sedan

A long, low sedan is the traditional language of business. It looks tailored. Its lines suggest restraint, and restraint suggests confidence. Getting in and out is easy and graceful, particularly in formal clothes, because you step across rather than climb up.

The ride is another strength. Sedans sit close to the road and tend to feel settled at speed, and many are designed with rear-seat passengers in mind. If your journey is mostly on good roads and you want to work, read or arrive looking composed, a sedan is hard to fault.

Consider one for:

  • Client meetings and boardroom appointments
  • Airport transfers for one or two travellers
  • Formal dinners and evening functions
  • Guests who prefer understatement

The case for the luxury SUV

An SUV has presence. You see it arrive. Its height gives passengers a commanding view and its size makes a clear statement at the entrance of a venue. It also offers practical advantages: a larger boot, more headroom and, on some models, a third row of seats.

In Kenya, SUVs have another clear argument. Not every memorable place is at the end of a smooth road, and a higher vehicle is often more comfortable on an uneven driveway or a track to a country venue. A 7-seater adds room for the whole party as well, which is why it suits weddings, family occasions and group transfers.

Consider one for:

  • Weddings and convoys
  • VIP guests and delegations
  • Families and groups with luggage
  • Upcountry trips and venues outside the city

Matching the car to the moment

The important first meeting

A dark executive sedan is the safe and handsome choice. It signals seriousness without demanding attention, and it lets the conversation be about the business in hand.

The visiting delegation

Several guests travelling together usually want to stay together, so an SUV or a matching group of cars tends to work better than scattering people across vehicles. Consistency looks organised.

The wedding

This is where SUVs often shine, particularly in a convoy. They photograph strongly, carry formal dress with ease and cope with garden venues. A flagship sedan can be a lovely choice for the couple's exit if you would like a contrast.

The gala

Consider the entrance. A flagship sedan brings classic elegance, while a large SUV brings drama. Either one works, so choose the one that suits the person getting out of it.

The weekend away

Look honestly at your bags, your passengers and your route. If the road is uncertain or the boot needs to be big, go for the SUV. If it is two people and a good highway, a sedan can be a delight.

Four practical checks

  1. Count the people, then count the bags. Luggage is the most commonly forgotten part of the calculation.
  2. Look at the destination. Check the road surface, the parking and the entrance.
  3. Think about clothing. Long gowns and high steps do not always get along.
  4. Consider who sits where. If your guest will be in the back, the rear seat matters more than the driver's view.

When you are torn

Describe the occasion to your rental company rather than simply asking for a type of car. Tell them who is travelling, where you are going and the impression you hope to make. A short conversation usually settles it. You can also use our compare tool to place up to three cars side by side and see how they differ.

Whichever you choose, the aim is the same. The car should fit the moment so well that nobody thinks about it twice, except to remember that you arrived beautifully.

title: Weekend Escapes from Nairobi: Travelling in Comfort
excerpt: A short break works better when the journey is part of it. How to plan a comfortable getaway, from choosing the car to packing the boot.
content:
One of the great pleasures of living in Nairobi is how quickly the city can be left behind. Lakes, highlands, forests and coastline all beckon, and a clear weekend is often all the excuse anyone needs. The difference between a restful break and a tiring one frequently comes down to how you travel.

Here is a general guide to planning a comfortable escape. Conditions and requirements change, so always check the latest information for your route before you set out.

Start with the shape of the trip

Before you book anything, decide what kind of weekend you actually want. Is the destination the point, with the drive simply a means of getting there? Or is the journey part of the fun, with stops along the way for a view, a meal or a market?

Be realistic about how far you want to go in the time you have. A destination that sounds wonderful can feel less so if you spend most of your break on the road. Ask friends who have made the trip recently, and check current travel information close to your departure.

Choosing a car for the road

Match the vehicle to the route and the party, in that order.

  • Good roads, two people. A comfortable sedan or compact SUV will be perfectly happy.
  • Family or friends with luggage. Consider a larger SUV, with a roomy boot and space for everyone to stretch out.
  • Rougher tracks or a remote lodge. Ask about a 4x4, and describe your route specifically when you do.

Before settling on a car, ask your lodge or host what the last part of the road is like. It is often the final stretch that determines what you need.

To drive or be driven

Driving yourself can be a pleasure when the road is open. Yet there is a good argument for a chauffeur if you want to arrive rested, if nobody in your group enjoys long drives or if the area is unfamiliar. It also means everyone in the car gets to look at the scenery.

Plan your departure well

Leaving Nairobi at the wrong moment can add a frustrating start to a relaxing weekend. Think about when the traffic in your part of the city tends to be heavy, and plan around it. Many travellers prefer to travel in daylight, particularly on unfamiliar routes, and it is a sensible habit to adopt.

Take breaks along the way. Stopping to stretch, have something to eat and swap drivers keeps everybody fresh, and some of the most enjoyable moments of a road trip happen at unplanned stops.

What to pack in the car

  • Your driving licence and identification, kept where you can reach them
  • Your rental documents and the company's contact details
  • Plenty of drinking water and some snacks
  • Phone chargers and a power bank
  • Offline maps, in case the signal fades
  • A warm layer, because evenings in the highlands can be cool
  • Some cash for small purchases and local charges
  • Sunglasses and sunscreen

If you are visiting a park or reserve

Parks have their own rules, entry arrangements and fees, and these do change. Check directly with the relevant authority or your lodge before you travel, and confirm that your vehicle is suitable for where you plan to go. Mention any such plans to your rental company when you book, so that they can advise you and confirm what is allowed for your car.

Before you hand back the car

Check the seats, the boot and the door pockets for anything you might have left behind. It is surprising how many sunglasses stay on holiday. Follow the return arrangements in your booking confirmation, and call if your plans change on the way back.

A few simple habits

  1. Tell someone your route and when you expect to arrive.
  2. Check the weather before you leave, especially in the rainy seasons.
  3. Save your support number somewhere you can find it easily.
  4. Drive to the conditions, not the schedule.
  5. Leave some of the weekend unplanned.

That last one may be the most important. The purpose of leaving the city is to stop being busy for a little while. Choose a car you will enjoy, set off at an easy hour and let the road do the rest.

title: Making an Impression: Luxury Cars for Business Meetings and VIP Guests
excerpt: Hospitality starts at the kerb. How to arrange transport for clients and important guests so that it reflects well on you.
content:
Every important guest forms an impression of your organisation long before the first meeting begins. It starts when they land, continues on the road and settles at the moment they step out at your door. Transport is one of the few parts of hospitality that a guest experiences entirely, from beginning to end, and it deserves more thought than it usually receives.

Whether you are hosting a single investor or a whole delegation, these are the things that make the difference.

Begin with the guest, not the car

Before choosing a vehicle, consider who is travelling. A senior visitor may want quiet and privacy. A team of colleagues may prefer to travel together and talk. Some people enjoy an imposing arrival, while others would rather slip in discreetly. Your assistant, their assistant or a quick question to the guest can settle this.

A few details are worth finding out in advance: how many people are coming, how much luggage they have, and whether anyone has particular needs or preferences for the journey.

Choosing the right level of presence

The car should match the occasion and the person, and more is not always better. A dark executive sedan is reliable, discreet and appropriate almost everywhere. A flagship sedan raises the sense of occasion, and it makes the rear seat the most comfortable place in the car. A premium SUV or a 7-seater brings height, room and presence, which works well for VIP events and for groups.

If you are transporting several people, a matching set of cars looks deliberate. It tells your guests that someone has thought about them.

Plan the whole movement

A guest's visit is rarely one journey. Write out every leg: the airport, the hotel, the office, lunch, dinner and the return flight. Then decide whether a single chauffeur-driven car for the whole visit would be simpler than booking separate trips.

Share the plan with your transport provider, and name one person on your side who can make decisions if anything changes. Most problems in hosting come from an unclear chain of communication rather than from the car.

Details that guests notice

  • Clear communication. Tell your guest in advance who is collecting them and how to find the car.
  • The right entrance. Know which door of the building you want them to arrive at, and tell the driver.
  • A quiet ride if they want one. Not everyone wishes to talk after a long flight.
  • Time to prepare. Share the agenda before the journey, so that the drive can be useful.
  • A contact number. Make sure your guest can reach someone who can help.

Discretion matters

Business conversations happen in cars. So do private phone calls and difficult decisions. When you are arranging travel for senior people, it is reasonable to ask how the provider handles personal information and to share only what is necessary to complete the booking. Keep itineraries for high-profile guests to those who need to see them.

Timing for a business day

A meeting missed because of traffic is an expensive way to save a little planning. Nairobi's roads can be unpredictable, so build in a comfortable margin, particularly for the first appointment of the day and the journey back to the airport. It is far better for a guest to arrive early and have a coffee than to arrive late and apologise.

After the meeting

The final impression counts as well. If your guest is heading to the airport or their hotel, make sure the car is ready when the meeting ends. A meeting can finish well, and then lose some of its shine if the visitor is left standing on the pavement wondering what happens next. Agree in advance how the driver will be told it is time.

A hosting checklist

  1. Note your guest's arrival details and preferences.
  2. Choose the car or cars that suit the occasion.
  3. Write out every journey during the visit.
  4. Confirm your quote and the arrangements in writing.
  5. Tell your guest how they will be collected.
  6. Name one person to manage any changes.
  7. Plan the departure as carefully as the arrival.

Most of this takes only a few messages to arrange, but your guest will feel the benefit throughout the visit. When transport is handled well, nobody mentions it. They just remember that everything went smoothly, and that you were the one who made sure it did.
